title: The Thank-You Letter You Never Sent
text:
Many people feel grateful to someone and never say so. In 2018 Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley of the University of Chicago looked at why.

They asked participants to write a short letter of gratitude to someone who had mattered to them, describing what that person had done and how it had affected them. Before the letters were delivered, the writers predicted how the recipients would feel: how surprised, how happy, and how awkward. Then the researchers contacted the recipients and asked how they actually felt.

The writers got it wrong in a consistent direction. They underestimated how surprised the recipients would be by the content, and how positive they would feel. They overestimated how awkward the recipients would feel. Recipients were often moved, and rarely uncomfortable. Writers also tended to worry about how well they had expressed themselves, focusing on finding the right words, while recipients focused on the warmth behind the letter. Because people expect thanks to land weaker and more awkwardly than it does, the researchers suggested, they hold back a simple act that would brighten someone's day and their own.
lesson: Thanks you never express does no good. Write the note or make the call; the other person will likely be happier and less awkward about it than you fear.
source: Kumar, A., and Epley, N. (2018). Undervaluing gratitude: Expressers misunderstand the consequences of showing appreciation. Psychological Science, 29(9), 1423-1435.
